'''Henry Ehrenreich''' (May 11, 1928{{Snd}}January 20, 2008) was an American physicist and [[Harvard]] professor who did research on [[semiconductors]] and [[solid-state physics]].

After fleeing Germany as a child, his family settled in [[New York (state)|New York]] where he attended university. He conducted research in a laboratory for [[General Electric]], and his expertise in semiconductors and the [[Materials science|physics of materials]] allowed him to advise two [[United States federal executive departments|US departments]]. As a [[professor]], he devoted much effort to improve the quality of education, eventually becoming the first [[ombudsman]] for Harvard.

==Personal life==
Henry Ehrenreich was born on May 11, 1928, in [[Frankfurt]] to [[German Jews]] Frieda and Nathan Ehrenreich. His father was a prominent pianist and [[choral conductor]], but in 1934 lost his position under the [[Nazi regime]] and was deported to [[Dachau]] in the wake of the [[Kristallnacht]]. He was released on December 7, 1938, and was able to flee Germany ten days later.<ref name="harvard-memorial">{{cite news |title=Henry Ehrenreich |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2010/02/henry-ehrenreich/ |access-date=December 7, 2020 |work=Harvard Gazette |date=February 18, 2010}}</ref>

Henry was able to flee Germany via the [[Kindertransport]], and was first taken to a foster home in England, but was soon sent to another foster home in [[Letchworth]] due to the [[Evacuations of civilians in Britain during World War II|evacuation of children from London]]. His German-speaking foster family there held Nazi sympathies and mistreated him. After his mother fled Germany on August 24, 1939, [[Outbreak of World War II|shortly before war broke out]], he was placed with another family in [[Ditchling]], where they could visit.<ref name="harvard-memorial"/>

The family finally obtained [[US visas]] in the fall of 1939, and was finally reunited in March 1940 in [[New York City|New York]]. His father found work two years later as a choral conductor in [[Buffalo, New York|Buffalo]] and Henry enrolled in high school there. A New York State scholarship allowed him to study at [[Cornell]] where he graduated in 1950. A year earlier, he met Tema Hasnas, and they married in 1953.<ref name="harvard-memorial"/>

Notwithstanding his decision to become a theoretical physicist, Ehrenreich shared a love for music with his father and was a skilled pianist.<ref name="harvard-announcement">{{cite news |title=Scientist, educator Ehrenreich dies at 79 |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2008/02/scientist-educator-ehrenreich-dies-at-79/ |access-date=December 7, 2020 |work=Harvard Gazette |date=February 7, 2008}}</ref> He was also an early adopter of e-mail and the [[History of the World Wide Web|World Wide Web]], despite already being considered an "elder of the faculty" in 1996. He stated that he got a [[PowerBook]] because Macs were "for idiots" and "kind of lick your hands and are friendly", but was still asking people in the hall for technical help.<ref name="crimson-cyberprof">{{cite news |last1=Macmillan |first1=Valerie J. |title=CYBER Prof |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1996/10/26/cyber-prof-pbgbregory-nagy-jones-professor/ |access-date=December 7, 2020 |work=The Harvard Crimson |date=October 26, 1996}}</ref>

He died on January 20, 2008, in [[Belmont, Massachusetts|Belmont]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Henry Ehrenreich Obituary (2008) - Boston Globe |url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/bostonglobe/obituary.aspx?pid=101631294 |website=www.legacy.com |access-date=December 8, 2020 |language=en}}</ref> leaving behind his wife Tema, his daughter, his two sons and 10 grandchildren.<ref name="harvard-announcement"/>

==Career==
After graduating, Ehrenreich studied at [[Columbia University]] for an academic year, returning to Cornell in 1951 where he began work as an assistant teacher. He took an interest in semiconductors and related problems, and started writing his doctoral thesis under [[Albert Overhauser]] on the "Scattering of Holes by Phonons in Germanium",<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ehrenreich |first1=H. |last2=Overhauser |first2=A. W. |title=Scattering of Holes by Phonons in Germanium |journal=Physical Review |date=October 15, 1956 |volume=104 |issue=2 |pages=331–342 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.104.331 |url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.104.331|url-access=subscription }}</ref> finishing it in 1955.<ref name="harvard-memorial"/>

To continue his research into surface and solid state science, he went to the [[General Electric Research Laboratory]]. During his time there, three children were born to the couple.<ref name="harvard-memorial"/>

He moved to [[Harvard University]] in 1960 and was appointed professor in 1963 at the [[Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences|Harvard Division of Engineering and Applied Sciences]]. His research coincided with the boom in semiconductor applications, and Ehrenreich authored over 200 papers over the course of his career. He also co-authored the annual review ''Solid State Physics'' together with [[Frederick Seitz]] and [[David Turnbull (materials scientist)|David Turnbull]].<ref name="harvard-memorial"/>

During the [[1973 oil crisis]], he was asked to assess solar [[Solar cell|photovoltaic cells]], served as an advisor to the [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]], and headed a study group on the matter from 1977 to 1981 before testifying to Congress in 1985.<ref name="harvard-memorial"/> He also served on the [[DARPA]] Materials Council of the [[United States Department of Defense|Department of Defense]] for 20 years, and participated in numerous national and international committees.<ref name="harvard-announcement"/>

Apart from his scientific contributions, Ehrenreich actively tried to improve Harvard [[undergraduate education]] in science and engineering and chaired the Core Committee on Science between 1987 and 1999.<ref name="harvard-announcement"/> When the Core Curriculum at Harvard came under scrutiny in 1989, he remarked: "The present system we have is working pretty well. But you can always ask if we can do better."<ref name="crimson-review">{{cite news |last1=Solowey |first1=Eric S. |title=Ten-Year Review Focuses on Mechanics, Not Philosophy |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1989/6/8/ten-year-review-focuses-on-mechanics-not/ |access-date=December 8, 2020 |work=The Harvard Crimson |date=June 8, 1989}}</ref>

Ehrenreich was also part of a committee that decided on [[Free Speech]] Guidelines at Harvard in the wake of an intense debate about a [[Modern display of the Confederate battle flag|Confederate Flag]] hung from a dorm room window in 1990.<ref name="crimson-debate">{{cite news |last1=Schugart |first1=Annie E. |last2=Vasquez|first2=Samuel |title=Political Correctness Debate Shook Harvard |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2015/5/27/political-correctness-debate-harvard/ |access-date=December 7, 2020 |work=The Harvard Crimson |date=May 27, 2015}}</ref> In February 2003, Ehrenreich and Lydia Cummings were appointed ombudsmen for Harvard university, promising a "safe haven" for people affected by problems stemming from the university, with the office remaining independent of Harvard's administrative structure.<ref name="harvard-ombudsmen">{{cite news |title=Ombudsmen open for business |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2003/02/ombudsmen-open-for-business/ |access-date=December 7, 2020 |work=Harvard Gazette |date=February 6, 2003}}</ref> They handled around 150 cases during the first year.<ref name="crimson-ombudsperson">{{cite news |last1=Habib |first1=May |title=Ehrenreich Sets Tone As First Ombudsperson |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2004/2/25/ehrenreich-sets-tone-as-first-ombudsperson/?page=1 |access-date=December 7, 2020 |work=The Harvard Crimson |date=February 25, 2004}}</ref>

Ehrenreich was critical of a distinction between "strategic" [[applied research]] and "curiosity-driven" [[basic research]], recounting the freedom to choose his own projects at the General Electric lab, and pointing to advances in semiconductor science that he saw as the result of an open stance towards basic research during the 50s.<ref name="halbleiterforschung">{{cite journal |last1=Ehrenreich |first1=H. |title=Halbleiterforschung in den 50er Jahren: Anwendungsorientierte Forschung und Zukunftstechnologie |journal=Physikalische Blätter |date=1997 |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=21–26 |doi=10.1002/phbl.19970530105 |s2cid=119595469 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/phbl.19970530105 |language=de |trans-title=Semiconductor research in the 1950s: application-oriented research and future technology |issn=1521-3722|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
